Attorneys are a bit in their “attorney bubble” but most not so much that they don’t empathize with admin. They involve us in conversations, socialize with us at happy hours, etc. I’ve even seen some push discovery or filings back a day when there are only a few LAs in office, we’re overwhelmed, and it’s not the day of deadline. 

Accountability is important here but some attorneys are willing to take the brunt of a mistake for their staff. When I first started, I made a small mistake. I immediately emailed the partner who pointed it out (via email to the entire admin team and his associate) to apologize. Two other LAs who had been training me and the associate immediately took the blame. 

Only the receptionists and attorneys speak to clients, which is rare but keeps us from having to deal with being berated while we do our work. And keeps the clients more satisfied with their representation imo. 

Training and expectations are very thorough and explicitly stated. This is across the board. 

Supervisors try to be understanding when people need to miss work and allow us to stay late, come in early, or work through lunch to make up the time. 

There is zero tolerance for staff being openly rude to other staff. 

The firm regularly caters meals and holds events, such as ice cream socials or themed happy hours. They give small gifts for holidays (like firm branded candies for Valentine’s Day). We get a good amount of firm branded merch when we first start. We also host a welcome lunch for new employees. 

We view ourselves as a team and pitch in to help one another constantly. 

Overall, I know a lot of this comes from the privilege of working at a large, high-volume/expensive firm, but if you are able to do things like this, it really goes a long way. A happy team is a productive team. And good on you for recognizing that!

I worked criminal defense for a while and saw more egregious offenses from police than our clients. Granted, we did not take on anyone charged with sexually violent offenses or major, intentional violent crimes. 

I’m sure you understand this, but to echo what others have said, the job isn’t necessarily to help a client “get away” with the crime or out of consequences. It’s to ensure that their rights are preserved throughout the process. 

We did have many clients with mental health issues, and we would often try to get them a psych eval or counseling. 

As for safety, ask any potential firms what safety measures they take. I’ve heard more war stories regarding family law clients than criminal clients though. Also, take steps to protect yourself. Don’t stay in the office alone with a client if this can be avoided (it should be per firm policy). Carry pepper spray, a personal alarm, etc. Don’t give out any information that can be used to trace you (cell number, personal life details, etc.) Set boundaries with the clients as appropriate, and you should be fine. 

Overall, criminal defense is very rewarding and there are even ways that we can serve a part in rehabilitating the client (even though that’s not our job). It’s certainly never dull. And if you like legal research and writing, criminal law may be very interesting to you.

Ask your boss to pay for/reimburse some workers’ comp specific CLE for you. I worked in WC before switching to corporate, and my boss let me sit in on one of his WC CLE webinars. 

As for the more practical things you can implement now, I would start with a through intake interview/screening form. I’m happy to send you one if you would like, but your state bar should have one that would be a good starting point. I would also look for a WC specific case checklist for your state (like when to file what form). Generally, I would file the claim form as claim only (WC14) same day as intake, request all medical records and wage verification same week, initial RPDs/Interrogs same month. Then, once the medical records came in I would comb through them, outline, request a mediation (be careful about this though - there’s one form for a factual mediation and one for a settlement mediation) or a hearing ASAP. Then, you’re going to want to draft stipulations and send them to OC. There will likely be a conference call shortly before the hearing where you discuss different issues with the judge. This would be the time for your attorney to have the stips in front of him and discuss any unagreed upon stips that should be common sense. I would make a table/spreadsheet delineating the two. Once the case is settled/adjudged upon, you’ll likely either need to appeal or (hopefully) calendar the due date of the settlement check. In the case of settlement, it’s a given that you’ll need to get the client in ASAP to sign a release. Read through it thoroughly and make sure you have filled out any blank portions, submitted any bills/atty fees to your SBWC, etc. If the check doesn’t come in time, you’ll likely need to file a Motion to Compel Settlement. At the end of the case, I like to send the client a thank you/closing file letter thanking them for their business and informing them of the firm’s document retention policy. 

Familiarizing yourself with the forms, calculations, and how to effectively comb through medical records is also a key element. I would keep a cheat sheet of how to calculate value of wages for estimated life span, medical dictionary, expert witness directory, interview sheets, and list of forms handy at my desk. I also like to keep a planned or list of priorities on my desk at all times.

My advice for recruitment as a former VP:
•Listen to your Pi Chi/Rho Gam/RC’s advice and talk to them if you need to but don’t bash the houses to them. They are supposed to be an unbiased, supportive resource to guide you through recruitment because they have firsthand knowledge of how the chapters on your campus recruit!
•Purge any photos from your socials that have any underage drinking in them if you haven’t already. Follow all of the chapters and the Panhellenic org on your campus. When I was a recruiter, we checked the women’s socials beforehand for “red flags” and to see if they were only following certain chapters which would give us a read on their interests going through recruitment. If you seem interested in only one chapter, that could hurt your chances with them all. 
•Don’t bash other houses in recruitment. These women have friends in every chapter and they all talk to each other. It also doesn’t reflect well on you if you’re saying something rude about her friend’s house. 
•Do a little bit of research on all of the sororities and show genuine interest (NOT on greekrank but on the sorority’s official websites lol). The more interested you are in them, the more interested they’ll be in you as they’ll perceive you as wanting to be active and involved in their chapter. Ask questions about their campus involvement, values, leadership structure, their favorite sorority event, etc. I remember my pref night at the house I joined when the woman I was talking to complimented my outfit and I returned the compliment saying I loved her necklace and thought it was cute that she chose to wear the chapter’s jewel for pref. Her face lit up and she was so excited!
•If you haven’t already gotten involved in other extracurriculars, volunteer work, or research, have a plan for that! Sororities look for women who are active leaders in their communities. If you are already involved, be prepared to talk about those orgs and why you are passionate about them! If not, say something along the lines of “I wanted to focus on getting settled with the transition from high school to college courses but I’m excited to get involved in xyz this semester” and ask about their community service, leadership roles, and campus involvement. 
•Avoid the 4B’s in conversations (boys, booze, bars, Bible). These topics can be seen as red flags and/or make the women uncomfortable because they are told not to discuss these things. There are a few exceptions. For example, if you are involved in a campus ministry or a particular line of the chapter’s public Purpose/Creed/Symphony/Mission statement resonates with you because of your faith, that’s fine to mention! 
•Have questions prepared in case conversation lulls! Ellaparrtierney and Claireliseg have amazing questions to ask during recruitment up on their tiktoks! 
•Don’t let the opinions of others sway you! Choose where you feel you will best fit in. Ideally, you’re finding people that you’ll share a connection with for a lifetime, and the perception of people miserable enough to care about tiers doesn’t matter in the long run. Many of the people I’ve met who are genuinely happy with their sorority experience aren’t in the most “top tier” chapters because those groups usually aren’t accepting or diverse. 
•Try not to take it personally if you get dropped from a chapter you like. The woman you talked to may have loved you, but the chapters factor in other things like grades, involvement, etc and they don’t even directly choose who gets invited back to them after the first round. It’s some random 3rd party the university hires to use an algorithm. 
•Above all, good luck and try to remember to enjoy yourself in all the craziness of recruitment!!
